course: Pizza Oven Construction - Wood Fired 12 Pizza

lessons.title: Excavation and Compaction for a Stable Base
lessons.body:
Start by marking the oven footprint on the ground with string and pegs. For a 12-inch pizza oven, the finished hearth is usually about 30 inches (76 cm) in diameter, but the foundation must be larger to support the dome and insulation. Plan a square foundation of at least 40 inches by 40 inches (100 cm x 100 cm). Dig a hole 12 inches (30 cm) deep across that entire area. Remove all loose soil, roots, and organic matter. In many parts of Africa, the soil can be sandy or clay-heavy; both need compaction.

Use a hand tamper or a heavy wooden post to compact the bottom of the hole. Compact in layers of 4 inches (10 cm) at a time. If the soil is very dry, sprinkle a little water to help it bind. For clay soils, you may need to add a 2-inch layer of crushed stone or gravel before compacting. This improves drainage and stability. Compact until the surface feels hard and does not move when you step on it.

Check the level of the compacted base with a spirit level and a straight board. The base should be flat and even. If it is not, add or remove small amounts of soil and re-compact. A stable base prevents the heavy concrete slab from cracking later. In areas with heavy rains, dig a small drainage trench around the hole to keep water out.

After compaction, you can optionally lay a plastic sheet or damp-proof membrane over the soil to stop moisture from rising into the concrete. This is especially important in humid regions. The sheet should cover the entire bottom and overlap the sides by a few inches. Now your base is ready for the concrete slab.

lessons.title: Pouring a Concrete Foundation Slab
lessons.body:
For a 40x40 inch foundation, you need about 0.5 cubic meters of concrete. Mix concrete using a ratio of 1 part cement, 2 parts sand, and 3 parts crushed stone (aggregate). Use a wheelbarrow or a mixing tray. Add clean water gradually until the mix is workable but not too wet. A good test: squeeze a handful; it should hold its shape without dripping water.

Build a wooden formwork (a frame) around the hole using 2x4 inch timber or plywood. The formwork should be level and sturdy. Oil the inside of the formwork lightly so the concrete does not stick. If you want a reinforced slab, place a grid of steel rebar (6 mm or 8 mm diameter) or wire mesh inside the formwork, about 2 inches above the ground. This helps prevent cracking.

Pour the concrete into the formwork in one continuous operation if possible. Use a shovel to spread it evenly. Then compact the concrete with a vibrating poker or by ramming with a wooden post to remove air pockets. Screed the top surface with a straight board to level it. The slab should be at least 4 inches (10 cm) thick. For a heavy oven, 6 inches (15 cm) is better.

Finish the surface with a steel trowel for a smooth top. Let the concrete cure for at least 7 days. Keep it damp by covering with wet sacks or plastic sheeting. In hot climates, cure for 10 days. This slow curing gives maximum strength. After curing, remove the formwork. The slab should be level and solid. This will be the base for your support structure.

lessons.title: Building the Support Structure (Concrete Blocks or Stand)
lessons.body:
The support structure raises the oven to a comfortable working height, usually 36 to 40 inches (90-100 cm) from the ground to the top of the hearth. You can build it with concrete blocks, bricks, or a steel stand. For a 12-inch pizza oven, a square or rectangular base is easiest. Use 6-inch (15 cm) concrete blocks. Lay the first course of blocks on the concrete slab using a mortar mix of 1 part cement to 4 parts sand. Make sure the first course is perfectly level; use a spirit level and adjust with small stones or mortar.

Build up the walls in a stretcher bond (overlapping the blocks). Leave a small opening at the bottom for an ash clean-out or storage. The walls should be at least 6 inches thick. For extra strength, you can fill every second hollow block with concrete and a piece of rebar. Continue building until you reach the desired height. Check level and plumb (vertical) as you go. If you are using a steel stand, weld or bolt together a frame from angle iron or square tubing. The top must be flat and strong enough to hold the heavy hearth.

On top of the support structure, you need a flat surface to build the hearth on. This is usually a second concrete slab, called the hearth slab. You can cast it in place or use a precast slab. The hearth slab should be at least 3.5 inches (9 cm) thick and reinforced with mesh. It should overhang the support walls by 2 inches on all sides. Make sure it is level. This slab will support the insulating layer and the firebrick floor.

Allow the mortar and concrete to cure for at least 3 days before adding weight on top. Keep it covered and damp. After curing, your support structure is ready for the insulating hearth layer.

lessons.title: Installing the Insulating Hearth Layer
lessons.body:
The insulating hearth layer stops heat from escaping downward into the concrete slab. Without it, your oven will take a long time to heat up and will waste wood. Use insulating materials that can withstand high temperatures. Common options in Africa include a mixture of perlite or vermiculite with cement, or ceramic fiber board. For a 12-inch oven, you need an insulation layer about 2 to 4 inches (5-10 cm) thick.

A practical mix is 5 parts perlite (or vermiculite) to 1 part Portland cement by volume. Add water until the mixture is like thick oatmeal. It should hold together when squeezed but not be soupy. Spread this mix evenly over the hearth slab to the desired thickness. Tamp it lightly with a float or trowel to compact it, but do not overwork it. The surface should be flat and level. Let it cure for at least 24 hours. It will be lightweight and crumbly, but that is fine because the firebrick floor will sit on top.

Alternatively, use ceramic fiber board, which is more expensive but provides better insulation and is easier to install. Cut the board to fit the hearth area and lay it flat. You can use two layers of 1-inch board for a total of 2 inches. Make sure there are no gaps between pieces. If using board, you do not need to cure it.

After installing the insulation, you must protect it from the weight of the firebricks. Some builders lay a thin layer of sand or a fireclay slip over the insulation to create a smooth bed for the bricks. This also helps level the floor. The insulating layer is critical for efficient wood firing. Do not skip it or use ordinary concrete, which will suck heat away.

lessons.title: Laying the Firebrick Hearth Floor
lessons.body:
The firebrick hearth floor is where you will bake your pizzas. It must be flat, smooth, and able to withstand high heat. Use dense firebricks (also called refractory bricks) that are rated for at least 1200Â°C. Do not use ordinary clay bricks or concrete blocks; they will crack. For a 30-inch (76 cm) diameter cooking surface, you need about 30 to 35 firebricks. Arrange them in a herringbone pattern or a running bond. Herringbone is traditional and looks good, but running bond is easier. The key is to have tight joints.

Before laying, make a bed of fine sand or a thin layer of fireclay mortar over the insulating layer. This helps level the bricks and fill any gaps. Lay the first brick at the center and work outward. Use a rubber mallet to tap each brick into place. Check level frequently with a spirit level. The bricks should be flush with each other. If a brick is too high, tap it down; if too low, add a little sand under it. For the best results, use a thin layer of fireclay mortar between bricks, but many builders lay them dry and then fill the joints with fine sand or ash. This allows for expansion.

After laying all bricks, fill the joints with a mixture of fine sand and fireclay (or just sand). Sweep it into the gaps. Then level the entire floor by rubbing a flat brick or a wooden block over the surface. You can also use a belt sander with a diamond pad, but that is not necessary. The floor should be smooth so that pizza dough does not stick. Any unevenness will cause hot spots and uneven baking.

Finally, cut the bricks around the edges to fit your oven's shape. You can use a masonry chisel or an angle grinder with a diamond blade. Take your time to get a neat edge. The firebrick floor is now ready for the dome, but first ensure it is perfectly level and clean.

lessons.title: Leveling and Smoothing the Hearth for Pizza Cooking
lessons.body:
A level hearth is crucial for even baking. After laying the firebricks, check the entire surface with a long spirit level (at least 24 inches). Place it in several directions: front-to-back, side-to-side, and diagonally. If you find high spots, mark them with a pencil. Use a rubbing brick (a piece of coarse firebrick) or a diamond grinding cup on an angle grinder to grind down high spots. Work slowly and check frequently. For low spots, you can lift the brick and add a little sand underneath, then re-lay it.

Once the floor is level, smooth the surface. Sweep away all dust and loose sand. Mix a thin slurry of fireclay and water (like milk) and brush it over the floor. This fills tiny cracks and pores. Let it dry, then sweep off any excess. Alternatively, you can rub the surface with a piece of smooth firebrick or a wooden block to polish it. The goal is a surface that feels like smooth concrete, with no bumps or dips.

A common mistake is to leave the floor too rough, which makes it hard to slide pizzas in and out. Another mistake is to have a floor that is not level, causing the pizza to cook unevenly. Take the time to get it right. You can test by placing a straight edge across the floor and shining a light from behind; any gaps should be less than 1 mm.

After leveling, clean the hearth thoroughly. Vacuum or sweep out all debris. Then you can proceed to build the dome. But before that, you may want to cure the hearth by building a small fire and gradually increasing the heat. This drives out any remaining moisture. Start with a small fire for 1 hour, then increase slowly over several days. This prevents cracking. Your hearth is now ready for baking perfect pizzas.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Building the Foundation and Hearth

In the African wood-fired pizza business, your oven is not just equipment â it is a revenue asset. A poorly built foundation means a cracked dome, uneven heat, and lost customers. This practical reference distils the six core lessons of this module into field-ready guidance for builders, entrepreneurs, and vocational trainees working in African conditions: high ambient temperatures, variable soil, limited water access, and the need to build with locally available materials.

The foundation and hearth determine three business outcomes: oven lifespan, fuel efficiency, and product consistency. Get them right and your oven will serve thousands of pizzas. Get them wrong and you will rebuild within a year.

1. Excavation and Compaction for a Stable Base

Begin by marking the oven footprint. For a 12-pizza wood-fired oven, allow a foundation slab of at least 1.2 m Ã 1.2 m (for a 90 cm oven) plus a 15 cm margin on all sides. Excavate to a depth of 20â30 cm, depending on soil. In much of sub-Saharan Africa, laterite and black cotton soils expand and contract with moisture â these require deeper excavation and a compacted hardcore layer.

Compact the subgrade in 10 cm layers using a hand tamper or plate compactor. Each layer should be watered lightly and compacted until it rings firm underfoot. A simple field test: drop a 5 kg weight from 30 cm; if it leaves a dent deeper than 5 mm, compact further. Skip this step and differential settlement will crack your slab and tilt your hearth.

2. Pouring a Concrete Foundation Slab

Use a 1:2:4 mix (cement : sand : aggregate) by volume. For a 1.2 m Ã 1.2 m Ã 0.10 m slab you need roughly 0.15 mÂ³ of concrete â about 50 kg cement, 0.1 mÂ³ sand, and 0.2 mÂ³ coarse aggregate. In hot African climates, work in the early morning, keep water clean, and cure the slab under damp sand or plastic for at least 7 days. Rapid drying causes surface crazing and reduces strength by up to 30%.

Embed a single layer of welded mesh (BRC) or 8 mm rebar at 150 mm centres, positioned mid-depth. This controls thermal cracking when the oven heats. Do not pour on uncompacted fill â that is the most common failure in small African workshops.

Table 1: Concrete mix and curing reference for a 1.2 m Ã 1.2 m oven slab
ParameterSpecificationNotes for African conditions
Mix ratio1:2:4 (cement:sand:aggregate)Use clean river sand; avoid salty beach sand
Slab thickness100â120 mmIncrease to 150 mm on black cotton soil
ReinforcementBRC mesh or 8 mm rebar @ 150 mmPosition at mid-depth, not on the ground
Curing time7 days minimum (28 days ideal)Cover with wet burlap or plastic; water 2Ã daily
Water:cement ratio0.5 by weightToo much water weakens slab â use a slump test

Source: Adapted from Concrete Practice, Cement & Concrete Institute (free technical notes), and FAO Small-Scale Construction guidelines.

3. Building the Support Structure

Two proven options: a concrete block stand or a steel stand. In most African towns, concrete blocks are cheaper and locally available. Build a rectangular base with 150 mm hollow blocks, filled with concrete at corners and every third cell. Leave a wood storage void underneath â this keeps fuel dry during the rainy season and increases oven efficiency.

If using a steel stand, use 50 mm Ã 50 mm angle iron welded into a frame, with a solid top plate. Steel is faster to install but requires a welder and anti-rust treatment. For a business that will operate daily for years, the block stand is the more durable choice.

4. Installing the Insulating Hearth Layer

The insulating layer sits between the concrete slab and the firebrick floor. Its job is to stop heat escaping downward â heat that should be cooking pizza. Use a 5â7 cm layer of perlite or vermiculite mixed with cement at 5:1 (perlite:cement) by volume, with just enough water to bind. Do not over-water; the mix should hold together when squeezed but crumble easily.

In Africa, perlite and vermiculite are available in most capital cities through horticultural suppliers. If unavailable, a 50 mm layer of dry sand or a double layer of ceramic fibre blanket can substitute, though with lower performance. Level this layer carefully â every bump telegraphs through to the firebrick above.

Table 2: Insulating hearth materials â performance and local availability in Africa
MaterialThicknessThermal conductivity (W/mÂ·K)Availability in Africa
Perlite-cement (5:1)50â70 mm0.10â0.14Horticultural suppliers, major cities
Vermiculite-cement (5:1)50â70 mm0.12â0.16Garden centres, some hardware stores
Ceramic fibre blanket25â50 mm0.05â0.08Industrial insulation suppliers, imported
Dry sand75â100 mm0.30â0.40Universally available, lower performance

Source: Thermal conductivity values from ASHRAE Handbook â Fundamentals (free summary tables) and Forno Bravo insulation guidance.

â  SAFETY WARNING â HEAT, LIME, AND SILICA

Cement and lime burns are common on African building sites. Always wear gloves, eye protection, and a dust mask when mixing. Perlite and vermiculite dust contains crystalline silica â do not breathe it; mix outdoors or wear an N95 mask. Never light a fire in the oven until the concrete and insulating layers have cured for at least 7 days and you have performed a slow, controlled drying fire over 2â3 days. A fast fire in a wet oven causes steam explosions that can send firebrick fragments flying. Keep children and customers at least 3 metres away during the first firing.

5. Laying the Firebrick Hearth Floor

The firebrick floor is the cooking surface. Use dense firebricks (not insulating firebricks) laid flat, tight-jointed, in a herringbone or running bond pattern. Herringbone is traditional and resists brick movement better under thermal cycling. Cut edge bricks with an angle grinder fitted with a diamond blade â do this outdoors with water suppression.

Lay bricks on a thin bed of fireclay mortar (1 part fireclay : 3 parts clean sand, mixed with water to a stiff paste). Tap each brick level with a rubber mallet. Do not use ordinary cement mortar â it will fail at pizza temperatures (400â500Â°C). In Africa, fireclay is available from brick suppliers and pottery workshops; if not, a 50:50 mix of fireclay and kaolin works.

6. Leveling and Smoothing the Hearth

After laying, check level in all directions with a spirit level and a straight edge. Any brick more than 2 mm proud will cause the pizza peel to catch and the base to burn unevenly. Rub high spots with a carborundum stone or a brick rub. Fill joints with fine fireclay slurry and wipe clean while damp.

Before first use, sweep the hearth, then heat slowly. A level, smooth hearth means your pizza slides effortlessly, cooks evenly in 90 seconds, and your staff can work at speed during peak evening trade. That is the difference between a profitable Friday night and a queue of impatient customers.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Excavate to 20â30 cm; compact in 10 cm layers until firm.
  • Pour 100â120 mm reinforced slab; cure 7 days minimum.
  • Build block or steel stand with dry wood storage underneath.
  • Install 50â70 mm perlite/vermiculite insulating layer, level.
  • Lay dense firebricks flat, tight-jointed, on fireclay mortar.
  • Check level with straight edge; rub down any high spots.
  • Fill joints with fireclay slurry; wipe clean before drying.
  • Cure 7 days, then dry-fire slowly over 2â3 days before cooking.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Small-Scale Construction and Food Processing Equipment
  • Forno Bravo â Free Pompeii Oven Plans and Hearth Construction Guide
  • Concrete Society (UK) â Free Concrete Practice Notes
  • ASHRAE â Free Technical Resources and Insulation Data
  • InterNACHI â Free Insulation and Thermal Performance Reference

This module is part of the Rise Africa Skills programme. Build once, build right â your oven is your business.

quiz.q: What is the recommended size for the foundation of a 12-inch pizza oven?
quiz.explanation: The foundation must be larger than the oven footprint, so 40x40 inches is recommended.

quiz.q: How deep should you dig for the foundation?
quiz.explanation: A depth of 12 inches provides a stable base for the concrete slab.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of compacting the soil before pouring concrete?
options: A) To make it easier to dig
B) To prevent the concrete from cracking
quiz.explanation: Compaction creates a stable base that prevents the heavy concrete slab from cracking.

quiz.q: What is the correct concrete mix ratio for the foundation slab?
quiz.explanation: A mix of 1 part cement, 2 parts sand, and 3 parts aggregate is standard for foundations.

quiz.q: How long should you cure the concrete foundation slab?
quiz.explanation: At least 7 days of curing is needed for the concrete to reach sufficient strength.

quiz.q: What is the recommended height for the support structure?
quiz.explanation: A height of 36-40 inches is comfortable for working with a pizza oven.

quiz.q: What type of blocks are commonly used for the support structure?
quiz.explanation: Concrete blocks are strong, readily available, and easy to work with.

quiz.q: Why should you fill some hollow blocks with concrete and rebar?
quiz.explanation: Filling with concrete and rebar adds structural strength to the support walls.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the insulating hearth layer?
options: B) To stop heat from escaping downward
C) To provide a smooth surface
quiz.explanation: Insulation prevents heat loss into the concrete, improving oven efficiency.

quiz.q: Which materials can be used for the insulating hearth layer?
quiz.explanation: Perlite (or vermiculite) mixed with cement is a common insulating material.

quiz.q: What is the correct ratio for a perlite-cement insulation mix?
quiz.explanation: A 5:1 ratio of perlite to cement by volume provides good insulation.

quiz.q: How thick should the insulating hearth layer be?
quiz.explanation: A thickness of 2-4 inches is sufficient for a 12-inch oven.

quiz.q: What type of bricks should be used for the hearth floor?
quiz.explanation: Firebricks are rated for high temperatures and will not crack.

quiz.q: What is a common pattern for laying firebricks on the hearth?
quiz.explanation: Herringbone is a traditional and strong pattern for hearth floors.

quiz.q: What should you use to fill the joints between firebricks?
quiz.explanation: Fine sand or fireclay allows for expansion and creates a smooth surface.

quiz.q: Why is it important to level the hearth floor?
options: A) To make it look nice
quiz.explanation: An uneven floor causes hot spots and uneven cooking.

quiz.q: What tool can be used to grind down high spots on the firebrick floor?
options: B) Rubbing brick or angle grinder
quiz.explanation: A rubbing brick or diamond grinding cup on an angle grinder can level high spots.

quiz.q: What is the final step after leveling the hearth?
options: B) Cure with a small fire
quiz.explanation: Curing with a small fire drives out moisture and prevents cracking.

quiz.q: How can you test if the hearth floor is level?
quiz.explanation: A long spirit level placed in multiple directions will show any gaps.

quiz.q: What is the maximum acceptable gap under a straight edge on the hearth?
quiz.explanation: Gaps should be less than 1 mm for a smooth cooking surface.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a damp-proof membrane under the concrete slab?
quiz.explanation: It prevents ground moisture from entering the concrete.

quiz.q: How long should you cure the support structure before adding weight?
quiz.explanation: At least 3 days of curing is needed for the mortar to set.

quiz.q: What is the recommended thickness of the hearth slab?
quiz.explanation: A 3.5-inch reinforced slab is sufficient to support the hearth.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of using ceramic fiber board for insulation?
options: B) It is easier to install
quiz.explanation: Ceramic fiber board has higher insulating value than perlite mix.

quiz.q: What can you use to cut firebricks to fit the oven shape?
options: B) Masonry chisel or angle grinder
quiz.explanation: A masonry chisel or angle grinder with diamond blade cuts firebricks.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using ordinary concrete for the insulating layer?
quiz.explanation: Ordinary concrete is not insulating and will draw heat from the oven.

quiz.q: What is the first step in building the foundation?
quiz.explanation: Marking the footprint ensures the hole is dug to the correct size.

quiz.q: What is the recommended thickness of the concrete foundation slab?
quiz.explanation: A 4-inch slab is minimum; 6 inches is better for heavy ovens.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a herringbone pattern in the firebrick floor?
options: B) To look traditional and strong
quiz.explanation: Herringbone is a traditional pattern that provides strength and aesthetic appeal.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find a low spot in the firebrick floor?
options: B) Lift the brick and add sand
quiz.explanation: Lifting the brick and adding sand underneath levels it.
